DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA comer Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: Ilwuw.dilg.com.ph DILG OPININ No. 49 s. 2023 JUL HON. CYRIL REO A. GLEPA, M.D. Municipal Mayor Municipality of Molave Province of Zamboanga Del Sur Dear Hon. Glepa: This has reference to your letter dated June 6, 2023 requesting legal opinion on the propriety of disposal through sale Lot No. 7844, which is owned by your municipal government, located in Barangay Madasigon, Molave, Zamboanga Del Sur. Based on the documents forwarded to the Department, it appears that the local government unit of Molave owns a residential lot [Lot No. 7884) located at Barangay Madasigan, at the back of Juanita Enterprises, but the same is designated as a playground and "outside the commerce of men" under the CLUP/town map. Currently, this lot was is being rented by Juanita Enterprises and has not been used for any other purpose. The current administration has decided to put the property for sale and to utilize the proceeds thereof for priority plans of the local government unit (LGU) such as housing project, demonstration farm of Agriculture Office among others. The Office of the Provincial Appraisal Committee recommended the amount of Php Fourteen Million, Two Hundred Nineteen and Four Hundred Ninety Pesos (Php 14, 219, 490.00) as the fair market value of Lot No. 7884 with an area of Three Thousand and Nineteen (3, 019) square meters. In view of the foregoing, you are asking the Department's legal opinion as to the propriety of disposing via sale Lot No. 7844, located at Barangay Madasigan, Municipality of Molave. At the outset, it is imperative to cite the provisions of Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991 which empowers LGUs to derive income from its properties, to wit: SECTION 18. Power to Generate and Abply Resources. - Local government units shall have the power and authority to establish an organization that shall be responsible for the efficient and effective implementation of their development plans, program objectives and priorities; to create their own sources of revenue and to levy taxes, fees, and charges which shall accrue exclusively for their use and disposition and which shall be retained by them; to have a just share in national taxes which shall "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

be automatically and directly released to them without need of any further action; to have an equitable share in the proceeds from the utilization and development of the national wealth and resources within their respective territorial jurisdictions including sharing the same with the inhabitants by way of direct benefits; to acquire, develop, lease, encumber, alienate, or otherwise dispose of real or personal property held by them in their proprietary capacity and to apply their resources and assets for productive, developmental, or welfare purposes, in the exercise or furtherance of their governmental or proprietary powers and functions and thereby ensure their development into self-reliant communities and active participants in the attainment of national goals. (emphasis supplied) In addition, Sec. 22 of the same law recognizes the corporate powers granted to a LGU which among others included the power to acquire or convey real or personal propertyl At this juncture, it may be relevant to stress that the real property of the LGU under consideration is designated as a playground and "outside the commerce of men" under the CLUP/town map. Article 422 of the Civil Code states that "[propeny of public dominion, when no longer intended for public use or for public service, shall form part of the patrimonial property of the State. " This provision of the Civil Code controls how public dominion property may be converted into patrimonial property susceptible to acquisition by prescription. After all, Article 420 (2) makes clear that those property "which belong to the State, without being for public use, and are intended for some public service or for the development of the national wealth" are public dominion property. For as long as the property belongs to the State, although already classified as alienable or disposable, it remains property of the public dominion if when it is "intended for some public service or for the development of the national wealth." Accordingly, there must be an express declaration by the State that the public dominion property is no longer intended for public service or the development of the national wealth or that the property has been convened into patrimonial. Without such express declaration, the property, even if classified as alienable or disposable, remains property of the public dominion, pursuant to Article 420(2), and thus incapable of acquisition by prescription. It is only when such alienable and disposable lands are expressly declared by the State to be no longer intended for public service or for the development of the national wealth that the period of acquisitive prescription can begin to run. Such declaration shall be in the form of a law duly enacted by Congress or a Presidential Proclamation in cases where the President is duly authorized by law2 It bears to note however that while we recognize the powers granted to LGUs in the exercise of their full autonomy, the same is subject to limitations provided in the Code and other applicable laws. Sec. 380 of the same law provides the rule on negotiated sale of property, to wit: SECTION 380. Negotiated Sale of Property. - Property no longer needed may also be disposed of at a private sale at such price as may be determined by the committee on awards, subject to the approval of the Commission on Audit or its duly authorized representative when the acquisition or transfer cost of the property exceeds Fifty thousand pesos (Php50,OOO.OO) in the case of provinces and cities, and Twenty-five 1 sec. ofthe LGC of 1991. 2 Republic of the Philippines vs. Emmanuel C. Cortez, G.R. No. 186639, February 5, 2014. Page 2 of 3

thousand (Php25,000.OO) in the case of municipalities and Barangays. In case of real property, the disposal shall be subject to the approval of the Commission on Audit regardless of the value or cost involved. In addition, Circular No. 2019-003 of the Commission on Audit (COA) re: Guidelines to Implement the COA Circular No. 2019-003 dated October 15, 2017 Amending Section 197, Title VI - Miscellaneous Provisions and Administrative Instructions of COA Circular No. 92-386 dated October 20, 1992 and Prescribing Additional Guidelines Thereon which laid out the guidelines to be observed in the request of LGUs for approval of the negotiated sale/disposal of real property prior to the perfection of the contract of sale. The subject circular also provided the documentary requirements needed for requests for approval of negotiated sale/disposal of real property by LGUs. Considering the foregoing, we respectfully recommend that the required documentary requirements set forth by the COA and the express declaration of patrimonial property be complied with before proceeding with the sale. Finally, this opinion of this Department is based solely on the facts and representations narrated from the letter and our appreciation of the same. Further, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you on this matter. Thank you.
